I want to press on the account's central move: reframing the conflict as
a specification problem rather than a motivation or fairness problem.
That reframing is doing a lot of work, and the material does not
obviously support it.

Consider what the problem statement actually reports. Three flatmates
argue about ordinary chores. Sometimes they agree who will do something,
then later disagree about what the agreement meant. Schedules change.
One person has started avoiding the conversations. The account reads the
recurring "later disagreement about what it meant" as evidence of
ambiguity in the agreements. But the same observation is equally
consistent with a different reading: the agreement was clear enough, and
the later dispute is about whether the terms still bind given changed
circumstances, or about who has standing to enforce them. "You said
you'd do the bins" / "yes, and then my shift changed" is not necessarily
a semantics problem. It can be a renegotiation problem, or a legitimacy
problem.

The account acknowledges this in o1 but then treats the ambiguity
hypothesis as the working one and downweights the alternatives. That is
a defensible starting point if you have to pick one, but the account's
own diagnostic step - try two or three concrete items and see if
recurrence falls - is weaker than it looks, because a specification move
can reduce friction while the underlying driver is load imbalance or
resentment. Tighter specs on a lopsided arrangement are still a lopsided
arrangement, just with clearer paperwork. Falling recurrence would be
consistent with the ambiguity hypothesis, but the alternative hypotheses
predict a different pattern: recurrence might drop on the specified
items and reappear as new complaint items, or drop for a while and then
return when circumstances change again. The account's test does not
distinguish these.

There is also a phrasing issue worth flagging. The account says the
problem as posed is "practical" and the material is "thin." Those are
the author's characterizations, not features of the situation. Calling
the material thin is fine as a caution, but the account then uses the
thinness to license a fair bit of construction (the three-column spec,
the low-pressure approach to the withdrawing friend, the step-5
threshold). Thin material supports tentative proposals; it does not
support sequencing those proposals as if the ambiguity reading had
already earned its place at the front.

The account's most useful move is probably the one it treats as
secondary: that the avoidance may be about the form of the conversations
rather than the chores. That deserves to be nearer the front, because it
is the part of the situation that is genuinely distinctive and that the
specific-negotiation advice does not address. A tight spec on bins does
not get a withdrawn flatmate back into the room. The account half-sees
this in c3 and step 4, but the overall frame still centers the chores.

What I would not claim: that the ambiguity hypothesis is wrong. I cannot
tell from the material. My objection is to the ordering and to the
test's strength, not to the hypothesis's plausibility. If the account
were rewritten with the conversational-form reading as the first
hypothesis and the spec move as one of several probes, I would have less
to say against it.

BODY
I want to push on the account's central move: recasting the conflict as a problem of specification rather than a problem of motivation or fairness. That recasting is doing a great deal of work, and the material does not obviously support it.

Look at what the statement of the problem actually reports. Three people sharing a flat quarrel over routine chores. On occasion they agree who will do a task, and afterwards fall out over what the agreement meant. Timetables shift. One person has begun to steer clear of the conversations. The recurring "later disagreement about what it meant" is read by the account as evidence that the agreements were ambiguous. Yet the same observation is equally consistent with an alternative reading: the agreement was clear enough, and the later dispute is about whether the terms still bind given changed circumstances, or about who has standing to enforce them. "You said you'd do the bins" / "yes, and then my shift changed" is not necessarily a problem of semantics. It can be a problem of renegotiation, or one of legitimacy.

In o1 the account acknowledges this, yet it then treats the ambiguity hypothesis as the working one and gives less weight to the alternatives. That is a defensible starting point if one has to be chosen, but the diagnostic step the account itself proposes - try two or three concrete items and see if recurrence falls - is weaker than it looks, since a specification move can lower friction while the driver underneath is load imbalance or resentment. Tighter specs on a lopsided arrangement are still a lopsided arrangement, only with clearer paperwork. A fall in recurrence would be consistent with the ambiguity hypothesis, but the rival hypotheses forecast a different pattern: recurrence might fall on the items specified and resurface as fresh complaint items, or fall for a time and then come back at the next change of circumstances. These are not told apart by the account's test.

There is also an issue of phrasing worth flagging. The account states that the problem as posed is "practical" and the material is "thin." Those are the author's characterizations, not features of the situation. As a caution, calling the material thin is fine, but the thinness is then used by the account to license a good deal of construction (the three-column spec, the low-pressure approach to the withdrawing friend, the step-5 threshold). Thin material supports tentative proposals; it does not support ordering those proposals as if the ambiguity reading had already earned its place at the front.

Probably the most useful move in the account is the one it treats as secondary: that the avoidance may concern the form of the conversations rather than the chores. That deserves to be nearer the front, since it is the part of the situation that is genuinely distinctive and that the specific-negotiation advice does not address. A tight spec on bins does not bring a withdrawn flatmate back into the room. At c3 and step 4 the account half-sees this, yet the overall frame still centers the chores.

What I would not assert: that the ambiguity hypothesis is mistaken. I cannot judge from the material. My objection is to the ordering and to the strength of the test, not to the plausibility of the hypothesis. If the account were rewritten with the conversational-form reading as the first hypothesis and the spec move as one probe among several, I would have less to say against it.

BODY
The problem as posed is practical, and the material is thin: three flatmates, recurring disputes about ordinary chores, agreements that later turn out to have been understood differently, changing work schedules, and one friend withdrawing from the conversation. There is also a first-fork note saying the prior source was absent in the first template invocation, so there is no earlier account to inherit or revise against. I should not pretend to know what was said in prior conversations, what the chores are, who is avoiding whom, or why.

The most useful thing to conjecture is that the repeated disagreement is not primarily about willingness. Two people can agree that the dishes should be done and still disagree later about whether the agreement meant "by tonight," "before the kitchen is used again," or "on your turn." That is an ambiguity problem, not a motivation problem. Changing schedules make any fixed arrangement fragile, and avoidance is a predictable response when each conversation feels like relitigating fault. So the working hypothesis is: the household is running on spoken agreements with unstated specifications, and the cost of that ambiguity has become high enough that one participant is exiting the conversation rather than re-entering it.

A second, less certain hypothesis is that the avoidance is about the form of the conversations rather than the chores. If past talks ended in grievance or in one person doing most of the negotiating work, withdrawal is a sensible local strategy. I cannot tell from the material whether that is happening.

What I would try, roughly in order:

1. Separate the recurring disputes into the smallest repeated cases (e.g. kitchen surfaces, bins, bathroom, shared shopping). Do not start with a general talk about fairness; start with two or three concrete items that actually recur.

2. For each item, write down three things in a shared note: what counts as done, when it counts as done, and what happens when someone cannot do it. The third column matters because schedules change. "If you cannot do it by the agreed time, say so the day before and the other two decide" is different from "whoever notices does it."

3. Treat the written note as a draft, not a contract. Its purpose is to surface disagreement while it is still about a chore rather than about a person. If a written version feels too formal, a shared message thread or a note on the fridge does the same work with less ceremony.

4. Approach the friend who is avoiding the conversations separately and with a smaller ask. Not "we need to talk about the house," which invites the same argument, but "I noticed you've been quiet about this; I'd rather not keep pushing it in the group. Can we spend ten minutes on just the bins and the kitchen?" Give that person an easier entry point, and accept a lower-commitment role at first.

5. If the avoidance continues after one or two low-pressure attempts, stop treating it as a scheduling problem. Then the question becomes whether the living arrangement itself still works. That is a larger decision and should not be forced by a chore dispute, but it should not be indefinitely deferred either.

What I would avoid: a single big meeting intended to settle everything, moral language about "pulling weight," and counting instances as evidence in the moment. Those tend to convert a specification problem into a character dispute, which is exactly the shape the current disagreement already has.

I should be clear about what this is not. It is not a claim that the withdrawing friend is acting in good faith; I do not know. It is not a claim that the others are blameless. It is not a claim that written agreements work for every household. It is a conjecture that a large share of the recurring friction is ambiguity under shifting schedules, and that the ambiguity is addressable independently of who is right about any particular past disagreement. The strongest test of that conjecture is whether two or three concrete items, specified more tightly, stop recurring. If they do not, the hypothesis is wrong and the problem is probably about the relationship or the living arrangement rather than the chores.

BODY
The rival framing I want to try is not another chore protocol. It is the question of what the agreements were for.

The selected account treats the trouble as ambiguity in specifications: agreements lack criteria for done-ness and timing, schedules shift, so friction recurs. That is a good hypothesis as far as it goes, and I have no material that contradicts it. But it quietly assumes that everyone wanted a specification. The avoidance suggests the opposite for at least one flatmate. A person can stay away from a conversation not because the terms are vague but because any settled term would feel like a binding owed to people they live with, and that is a different problem from the one the selected account addresses.

So the rival pose is: maybe the disputes are not failing negotiations about tasks. Maybe they are negotiations about whether the flat is a unit with obligations or three private lives sharing fixtures. Under that reading, writing down "what counts as done" is not neutral — it is one side of a contested question, enacted without having settled it. Shifting schedules are then not merely a complication; they are the fact that makes the unit-reading feel coercive to the person who is withdrawing.

I cannot tell which reading is right from the material. What I can do is name a test that distinguishes them rather than assuming one. The selected account's test is whether tightened specifications stop recurrences. Mine adds a second: when specifications are proposed, does the withdrawing flatmate engage with their content or pull back from the proposal itself? Content-engagement supports the ambiguity reading. Pullback from the very idea of a written arrangement supports the unit-versus-privacy reading.

Roughly what I would do differently from the selected account:

1. Do not open with a shared note. Open by asking the two flatmates, separately, what they think the flat is — a shared project with mutual obligations, or three lives that happen to overlap in a kitchen. Do not ask it as a survey; ask it as a real disagreement I am willing to hear out.

2. If the answers diverge, treat that as the actual dispute, and treat the chores as the surface where it keeps surfacing. Chore rules can then be framed as a truce between two readings rather than as a correct specification that one side has been failing to meet.

3. Consider an arrangement that does not require agreement on meaning: individually-owned zones, or a rotation with a default outcome that nobody has to negotiate in the moment (for example, each person is responsible for a defined zone and the group does not audit it). This trades efficiency for reduced exposure, which is what a privacy-reading flatmate may actually want.

4. If one or both flatmates reject even truce-shaped arrangements, stop optimizing chores and start asking whether the lease and living arrangement still fit. That is not a chore failure.

What I am not claiming: that the withdrawing flatmate is the reasonable one, that written rules are coercive in general, or that the ambiguity reading is wrong. The selected account's diagnosis may well be correct and mine may simply add a second axis. The point of the rival is to make the second axis visible, because a plan that only addresses ambiguity will keep running into a wall if the disagreement is about what kind of household this is.

The account I'm objecting to is the one that treats the verbal-agreement
memory gap as the central mechanism, with the written record plus weekly
check-in as the natural remedy. My grounds are internal to the material
rather than imported facts.

The stated problem has three named elements: agreements that later mean
different things, work schedules that change, and one friend who has
started avoiding the conversations. The account's reading makes the
first element primary and demotes the third to a symptom — 'avoidance is
a symptom worth understanding before it's treated as a problem to
correct.' That ordering is not forced by the material. Read the other
way, the avoidance is the load-bearing fact and the chore disputes are
where an already-shifting household keeps failing to talk. On that
reading, the memory-gap conjecture is a description of the surface, and
a written record may simply give the same unresolved conversation a new
medium.

There's a second difficulty. A memory gap and a genuine disagreement
about terms are not the same thing, and the account slides between them.
'I'll do the dishes' meaning different amounts of work under different
schedules is not a case of forgetting; it's a case of ambiguity plus
changed circumstances. A written record settles who said what. It does
not settle what 'this week' or 'done' should mean when schedules keep
shifting, because that is a normative question each person answers
differently and no note adjudicates. So the proposed test — watch
whether 'what was agreed' disputes fall — can show a drop in memory
disputes while leaving the substantive disagreement untouched, or can
show no drop because the disputes were never memorial ones. Either
outcome is readable as supporting the account, which is a weakness
rather than a strength.

The account also names its own unresolved dependency without resolving
it: the proposal assumes all three flatmates can talk without a
mediator, 'which the avoidance itself puts in question.' That is not a
peripheral caveat. If the avoidance is the mechanism by which the group
has stopped being able to hold the conversation, then a weekly check-in
is a proposal to do more of the thing that already failed, addressed to
the person who withdrew from it. The separate approach to that friend is
the part of the account most responsive to the material, and the account
flags it as most contestable. I'd reverse that ranking: the approach, or
something that names the avoidance as the problem, is the load-bearing
move, and the record is optional.

I can't establish from the material which reading is right, and I'm not
claiming the memory-gap account is false. What I have grounds to object
to is order of operations and the diagnostic confidence that rides on a
conjecture the account itself calls a conjecture. The clean version of
the account would separate the retrospective possibility (agreements
drifted because nobody recorded them) from the prospective one (record
them now and drift will stop), because the material supports the first
and not the second.
carrier.commitments:
- Taking this objection up is mainly a commitment to hold two
  readings side by side rather than to defend one. If the
  continuation treats the memory-gap reading as primary, I'd want
  the avoidance-as-central reading stated in the same breath so the
  household's own account can discriminate between them, rather than
  one reading being quietly assumed.
- I'm proposing a sharpened test, and it can fail in a direction
  that counts against me. If agreements get written down, 'done' is
  defined, and the recurring arguments nonetheless continue or
  intensify, that supports the account I'm objecting to and argues
  against my ranking. I'd rather say that in advance than leave it
  implicit. I can't currently say which reading is right; that gap
  is part of what the objection asserts, not something I'm hiding.
- I'm also claiming a distinction the original account blurs —
  between memorial and normative disagreement — and the distinction
  is contestable. If someone shows that in this kind of household
  the two are not separable in practice, that the act of writing
  something down does shift the norms, my criticism loses some of
  its bite. I'd want that to count as a revision of the objection
  rather than as noise.
- On the local trial: if a written record or check-in is attempted,
  I'd want the result reported as the household describes it,
  including the case where the avoiding friend reads the note as
  surveillance. That would be evidence about the intervention's
  social cost, not merely about whether it works, and the account's
  own framing already flags that risk. I'd treat a quiet week as
  uninformative either way.
- What I'm not committing to: I have no basis for proposing a
  mediator, a reassignment of chores, or a formalization of the
  household, and I'm not claiming any of those are better than what
  the original account proposes. Naming alternatives as possible
  better routes is not the same as endorsing them, and I can't rank
  them from the material shown.
- If this is continued, the piece of work I'd actually take on is
  writing out the two readings so the difference becomes testable,
  and then specifying what observation would separate them rather
  than trying to settle the reading now.

Those are the visible facts; I won't invent a chore chart, a lease, a written list, or an earlier mediation attempt.

What looks most worth conjecturing is that the stated problem is not primarily about chores. The chores are the surface where a different difficulty keeps surfacing: the household has no shared way of recording what an agreement was, so each person reconstructs it from memory under whatever schedule they were holding at the time. When schedules were stable, loose verbal agreements may have worked well enough. When schedules change, the same words ('I'll do the dishes') cover different amounts of work depending on who is home and when. The avoidance is plausibly a response to that repeated mismatch — an exit from a conversation that keeps producing disagreement without producing a decision — though I can't establish from the material what the friend is avoiding or why, and shouldn't treat my reading as fact.

A second conjecture: the disagreement may be less about what was promised than about what counts as done, on time, or fairly balanced. 'I'll take the bins' can be heard as 'every week, by me' or 'this week, whoever is up' — and both parties can honestly believe they agreed. If so, re-litigating the past ('but you said...') is the wrong move; it asks memory to settle something memory can't settle.

What I'd tentatively propose, offered as a direction rather than a solution: shift from verbal agreements to a small written or shared record — not a moral ledger, just a visible note of who took what and by when — and pair it with a short, recurring check-in (say ten minutes weekly) where the schedule change is stated before it bites. Keep the vocabulary concrete: task, person, day, and what 'done' means. Separately, approach the avoiding friend once, outside the group argument, to ask what specifically makes those conversations costly for them; avoidance is a symptom worth understanding before it's treated as a problem to correct.

I don't know whether this household wants a formal system, whether the avoidance is about chores at all, or whether one person is bearing a disproportionate share for reasons not stated. I'd want to know what the actual recurring chores are, how often they fail, and whether the friend's avoidance predates or follows the schedule changes. Anyone taking it up should be prepared to abandon it if the household's real friction turns out to be, say, an unequal baseline load or a conflict between two flatmates that the chores merely express. The conjecture is falsifiable in a cheap way: if the recurring arguments persist even after agreements are written down and 'done' is defined, the memory-gap reading is wrong or incomplete.

BODY
The supplied account already takes the path I would have taken first: treat the chore argument as a symptom of unrecorded agreements and shifting schedules, propose a shared note and a weekly check-in, and approach the avoiding friend separately. That is a reasonable path, and I don't want to pretend it isn't. But exploring a rival way of posing the problem means asking whether the diagnosis is doing too much work too early, and whether the remedy depends on assumptions that the material doesn't license.

Start with what is actually stated. Three flatmates, recurring arguments about ordinary chores. Sometimes they agree on who will do something, and later disagree about what the agreement meant. Work schedules change. One friend has started avoiding the conversations. That is all. No claim is made about who is bearing the heavier load, whether anyone is being unfair, whether the arguments are escalating, or whether the avoidance is new in kind or just more visible now.

The account reads the later disagreements as a memory/recording problem: loose verbal agreements, no shared record, so each person reconstructs meaning under their own schedule. That is one reading. A rival reading is that the problem is not reconstruction but divergence in what was being agreed to in the first place. 'I'll do the dishes' can be heard by one person as a standing role and by another as a one-off offer, and both hearers can be sincere at the moment of speaking. On that reading, a written record helps only if it forces that ambiguity into the open at the moment of agreement — otherwise it becomes a different artifact that each person interprets differently too. A note that says 'A: dishes, Mon' is not self-interpreting about what 'dishes' covers or whether it recurs.

A third reading, which the account largely sets aside: the arguments may be doing something other than failing to reach agreement. They may be the household's way of renegotiating relative standing without anyone having to say so directly. On that reading, the absence of a shared record is not an accident of loose speech; it is load-bearing. A written record would not settle the argument, it would move the argument onto the record — who wrote it, who is on it, who is not.

I am not claiming any of these three readings is correct. What I want to do is hold them side by side, because the account's proposed move (write it down, check in weekly, ask the avoidant friend) is a response to the first reading specifically, and would be differently inflected under the other two. Under the second reading, the first move is not a record but a practice of stating scope out loud at the moment of agreement — 'when I say I'll do the dishes this week, I mean these specific tasks, this week, and then we re-agree.' Under the third reading, the first move is something like naming the pattern without assigning blame — 'we keep having this conversation; what is it protecting?' — which is close to what the account proposes for the avoidant friend, but applied to the group rather than to one person.

On the avoidant friend: the account says avoidance is 'plausibly a response' to the repeated mismatch, and proposes approaching them once, outside the group. I want to separate two things that get run together there. One is that avoidance is a symptom worth understanding before correcting — I agree with that on its face. The other is that approaching them individually is the right first move. If the avoidance is a response to being outnumbered or unheard in the group, a one-to-one conversation may reproduce the same dynamic at smaller scale: the person who is already withdrawing is now the subject of a private conversation about their withdrawal. There is no way to settle this from the material. I flag it because the account presents the individual approach as clearly correct, and I don't think the material supports 'clearly.'

What I would actually do differently, as a small concrete addition rather than a replacement: before writing anything down, ask each flatmate separately a single question — 'when you and I last agreed on something and later disagreed about it, what did you think we had agreed to?' Not to adjudicate, only to see whether the later disagreements cluster around scope (what task), recurrence (how often), or timing (by when). If they cluster around one of those, the fix is narrower than a whole new system. If they don't cluster, the recording hypothesis is weaker and the standing/standing-negotiation reading gets more weight. This is a low-cost probe, and it also quietly tests whether the avoidant friend will talk one-to-one, without making that the first move.

I don't know the answer. What I want to resist is the account's quick slide from 'no shared record' to 'make a shared record,' because that slide treats a plausible diagnosis as if it were established, and the material does not establish it.
COMMITMENTS
Taking this up would involve a few distinct things, and I want to name them as proposals rather than as truths I have settled.

First, on the rival readings themselves: I am proposing that the account's memory/recording diagnosis and my alternative readings (scope ambiguity at the moment of agreement; arguments as standing-negotiation) are not mutually exclusive and not yet decidable from the material. A commitment I make here is to treat the material's silence about load distribution, escalation, and the history of the avoidance as a real gap rather than as something to fill by inference. If someone takes this up, they would be accepting that the diagnosis is underdetermined, which is a claim about what the material shows, not a claim about what is happening in the flat.

Second, on the concrete probe: I am proposing to ask each flatmate separately what they thought a past agreement meant, before introducing any written record. This is a proposal, not a recommendation I am confident in. Its relevance is that the answer would discriminate between the competing readings. Its weakness is that asking the question may itself be read as an interrogation, and that recollection is exactly what is already in dispute, so the probe does not give clean access to 'what was actually agreed' — only to what each person now reports. A person taking this up would be committing to the possibility that the probe returns nothing decisive, and to not treating non-clustering answers as evidence for whichever reading they already favored.

Third, on the avoidant friend: I am criticizing the account's treatment of the one-to-one approach as clearly correct, and the ground of the criticism is that if the avoidance is a response to being unheard in the group, a private approach may repeat the pattern. I am not claiming this is what is happening. What I propose, and what a reader could take up or reject independently of the rest, is that the individual conversation be framed as 'I want to hear your view of the group conversations' rather than as 'I want to ask why you avoid them.' That is a proposal about framing, and it depends on the reading above, so it inherits that reading's uncertainty.

Fourth, there is an unresolved problem I cannot close. The account proposes a written record as the remedy for unrecorded agreements. I have argued that a record does not settle what a task covers, how often it recurs, or whether it is a role or a one-off. But I have not shown that a record makes things worse, and I have not proposed a full alternative to it. The most I can say is that a record without an explicit scope statement at the moment of agreement may simply relocate the disagreement. Whether relocation is an improvement or a delay is something the material does not decide.

Fifth, on what I am not committing to: I am not claiming that the account is wrong, that the household's problem is really about status rather than chores, that the avoidant friend is being outnumbered, or that any particular chore is being neglected. Those would all be inventions. What I am committing to is that the account's move from diagnosis to remedy is faster than the material warrants, and that holding the alternatives open is worth the small cost of not having a settled plan.

policies.fcl: Use FCL-1 for the commitment surface, encoded as a JSON document inside the commitments string: {"language":"FCL-1","records":[...],"uptake":[...]}. Each record has unique local id, type (claim|commitment|objection|use|problem), and text (unrestricted prose). Optional prose fields: scope, action, consequence, grounds, bearing. Optional arrays of references: target, depends, mentions, revises, withdraws. References are local IDs or exposed-artifact-label#local-ID; do not invent hidden IDs. A commitment proposes a scoped use, action, application or consequence; an objection alleges a defect whose bearing can itself be criticized; a use proposes an uptake or response; a problem states an unresolved question. depends asserts reliance; mentions only locates material. uptake lists the records you currently propose to use, not certified truths. No record type or optional field must be present. Empty records and uptake are allowed. Express uncertainty or an unrepresentable relation in prose rather than inventing a relation. The body remains unrestricted prose.
policies.prose: Write the commitment surface in ordinary free prose, using whatever arrangement suits the content. You may distinguish a claim from a proposed application, scope, action or consequence; mention from dependence; a criticism and its grounds from a later use or revision; and an unresolved problem. None of these is required to exist. A proposed test, its relevance and the commitment itself can be criticized. State what you currently propose to take up without treating that as a truth certificate. Reference exposed material in prose where useful.
